title: Knife skills
summary: Grip, guiding hand and a small set of cuts held to a consistent size, so every piece on the board cooks at the same rate.

misconceptions.text: A sharp knife is more dangerous than a dull one.

explain: names the pinch grip and the clawed guiding hand and says what each one controls
explains why a dull blade slips off the skin of an onion where a sharp one bites
states why uniform size matters more than the shape of the cut
apply: cuts a brunoise, a julienne and a batonnet within about a millimetre of the standard size
keeps the tip on the board and cuts with a forward slicing stroke rather than chopping down
hones the edge on a steel between tasks and stops to sharpen when honing stops working
discriminate: separates honing, which realigns the edge, from sharpening, which removes steel
separates a dice from a mince by the finished size and by what the cut is for
separates slicing across the grain from slicing with it and says what each does to texture

title: Heat control
summary: Matching the energy under the pan to what the food needs: a rate of heat transfer you steer by sound, colour and smell, not a number on a dial.

misconceptions.text: Turning the heat up always cooks the food faster.

explain: distinguishes conduction, convection and radiation and gives one pan example of each
explains why a heavy pan holds a steadier surface temperature than a thin one
explains what happens to the pan surface the moment cold food lands in it
apply: preheats a heavy pan to roughly 190 to 200 C for a sear and lets it recover between batches
holds a simmer at 85 to 95 C without letting it break into a rolling boil
adjusts the flame in response to the sound in the pan rather than to a fixed setting
discriminate: separates the heat going into the pan from the temperature inside the food
separates shimmering oil, a first wisp of smoke and a scorching pan as three different states
separates a sear, which needs high dry heat, from a sweat, which needs low covered heat

title: Mise en place
summary: Everything measured, cut and placed within reach before the first pan goes on, so that cooking is execution rather than searching.

misconceptions.text: Prep is dead time you can save by starting the pan earlier.

explain: lists what a station holds: prepped components, tools, waste bin, towels and a wiped rail
explains why the layout of the station follows the order of the cooking
explains how prep moves decisions out of service and into the quiet part of the day
apply: writes a prep list ordered by longest lead time first and works it from the top
sets a station so every component of the dish is reachable without stepping away
resets and wipes the station between courses instead of only at the end of service
discriminate: separates mise en place from simply prepping ingredients in advance
separates a station reset from a deep clean
separates a hold-up caused by missing prep from one caused by oven or burner space

title: Cooking ratios
summary: The fixed proportions by weight underneath a recipe: 1:1 roux, 3:1 vinaigrette, a 5 percent brine, 3:2:1 shortcrust. They scale where a cup measure does not.

misconceptions.text: Measuring flour by the cup is as reliable as weighing it.

explain: states at least three working ratios by weight and what each one produces
explains why a ratio by weight survives scaling where a volume measure drifts
says which ingredient in a ratio is the reference and which one moves
apply: scales a 3:1 vinaigrette from 60 g to 900 g without rebuilding the recipe
weighs a 1:1 roux and reads a finished sauce back to about 100 g of roux per litre
brines at 5 percent salt by weight of water and sets the time by the thickness of the cut
discriminate: separates a ratio from a recipe by what stays fixed when the yield changes
separates baker's percentage, where flour is 100 percent, from a percentage of the total weight
separates a ratio that holds by weight from one that only works at one scale by volume

title: Seasoning
summary: Salt used in layers through the cooking, judged by weight, around 1 percent of the food for most savoury dishes, and confirmed by tasting at every stage.

misconceptions.text: Salt belongs at the end, so the dish does not get too salty.

explain: explains what salt does to perceived sweetness and bitterness, not only to saltiness
explains why salt added early has time to diffuse into the food
gives a working target by weight, about 1 percent for most savoury food
apply: seasons in layers and tastes at each stage instead of once at the pass
weighs salt for a brine or a forcemeat rather than measuring by pinch
brings a flat dish back by changing one thing at a time and naming which one it needed
discriminate: separates a dish that is under salted from one that is flat and needs acid
separates seasoning by weight from seasoning by taste and says when each is used
separates fine salt from coarse salt by weight for the same spoon

title: Maillard reaction
summary: The browning between amino acids and reducing sugars that runs usefully on a dry surface above about 140 C and builds the crust, the fond and most of the aroma.

misconceptions.text: Searing meat seals in the juices.

explain: states what the reaction needs: amino acids, reducing sugars and a dry surface above about 140 C
explains why a wet surface stalls near 100 C until the water has gone
says what browning actually adds, which is colour and aroma rather than sealed in moisture
apply: dries and salts the surface, then sears in a pan held near 200 C without crowding it
leaves the protein alone until it releases from the pan instead of moving it early
keeps the fond in the pan and builds the sauce on it
discriminate: separates Maillard browning, which needs protein, from caramelization of sugar alone
separates a crust built by dry heat from a colour built by a sugar glaze
gives one case where a seared piece of meat loses more juice than an unseared one

title: Caramelization
summary: The thermal breakdown of sugar on its own, starting near 160 to 170 C for sucrose, which builds colour and then bitterness with no protein involved.

misconceptions.text: Onions caramelize in ten minutes over high heat.

explain: gives an approximate onset for sucrose, about 160 to 170 C, and what happens past deep amber
explains why the last twenty seconds of a caramel change it more than the first two minutes
explains how a wet caramel and a dry caramel behave differently in the pan
apply: takes a dry caramel to a deep amber and stops it with cream or butter off the heat
cooks onions slowly with a little salt for roughly 40 minutes, deglazing as fond builds
reads colour and smell to stop the pan a moment before it turns bitter
discriminate: separates caramelization from Maillard browning by what is reacting
separates genuinely caramelized onions from onions merely browned in ten minutes
separates a seized caramel from a crystallized one and gives the fix for each

title: Blanching
summary: A short plunge into heavily salted boiling water followed by an ice bath, to set colour, loosen skins or part cook a vegetable for a fast pickup.

misconceptions.text: Blanching water only needs a small pinch of salt.

explain: states the purposes: fix the colour, stop enzyme activity, part cook for service
explains why the water must be at a rolling boil and salted to about 1 percent
explains why the ice bath is part of the technique rather than an optional extra
apply: blanches green vegetables in water salted to about 10 g per litre and shocks them within seconds
works in batches small enough that the water comes back to the boil quickly
drains and dries the vegetables before storing so they do not sit in water
discriminate: separates blanching from poaching by temperature and by intent
separates shocking in ice water from simply draining and cooling on a tray
separates a vegetable blanched for a pickup from one cooked all the way through

title: Poaching
summary: Cooking gently in liquid held below a simmer, roughly 60 to 80 C, so delicate proteins set without tightening, curdling or breaking apart.

misconceptions.text: Poaching liquid should hold a gentle bubble.

explain: gives the working range, about 60 to 80 C, and says what a bubble at the surface means
explains why an egg white sets near 62 C and the yolk near 65 C
says what the poaching liquid contributes: seasoning, acid and aromatics
apply: holds the pot at 70 to 75 C and corrects the flame before the surface breaks
poaches fish to an internal 50 to 55 C and lets it rest in the warm liquid
seasons the poaching liquid so the finished piece is seasoned through, not only on the outside
discriminate: separates poaching from simmering and boiling by temperature and by surface movement
separates poaching from blanching by intent and by how the food is finished
separates a protein that is just set from one that is overcooked and grainy

title: Roasting
summary: Cooking in dry oven heat, where the surface browns while the core climbs slowly, managed with oven temperature, a probe, resting and carryover.

misconceptions.text: Resting a roast only lets it go cold.

explain: explains carryover cooking and why a roast comes out below its target temperature
explains why a rack and a dry surface matter more than frequent basting
explains what resting does to the juices and to the internal temperature
apply: pulls a chicken at 71 C in the thigh, or a beef rib at 52 C for medium rare, and rests it
uses two oven stages, hot for colour and moderate to finish, or the reverse
probes at the thickest point away from bone and confirms with a second reading
discriminate: separates roasting from braising by the cooking medium and the texture aimed at
separates oven temperature from the internal temperature of the food
separates a roast that needs more time from one that only needs more colour

title: Braising
summary: Browning first, then cooking partly submerged at 85 to 95 C until collagen becomes gelatin, usually two to four hours for a working cut.

misconceptions.text: A braise cooks faster at a hard boil.

explain: explains collagen turning to gelatin above about 70 C given enough time
explains why the liquid comes part way up the meat rather than covering it
explains why a hard boil tightens the muscle fibres and dries the meat out
apply: browns the cut hard, deglazes, then holds the oven at 150 to 160 C for a bare simmer
tests doneness with a probe that slides out without resistance rather than by the clock
cools the meat in its liquid and lifts the set fat off the next day
discriminate: separates braising from stewing by the size of the pieces and the depth of the liquid
separates braising from roasting by the transfer medium and the finished texture
separates meat that is still tough because it is underdone from meat dried out by too much heat

title: Reduction
summary: Boiling water out of a liquid to concentrate flavour, gelatin and body, which concentrates salt and acid at the same rate.

misconceptions.text: Any thin sauce can be fixed by reducing it further.

explain: explains that a reduction concentrates salt and acid along with the flavour
explains what gelatin from a stock does to body as the liquid falls
explains why a wide pan reduces faster than a tall narrow one
apply: reduces wine and stock by about half and reads the body on the back of a spoon
seasons after the reduction rather than before it
keeps a lively simmer in a wide pan and stops while the sauce still moves freely
discriminate: separates thickening by reduction from thickening by starch or by emulsion
separates a sauce that is thin from one that is simply under seasoned
separates a correct reduction from one that has gone sticky and oversalted

title: Emulsions
summary: Fat held as droplets in water, or the reverse, kept apart by an emulsifier such as mustard, egg yolk lecithin or the proteins in butter.

misconceptions.text: Once an emulsion holds, it is stable and can be boiled.

explain: names the three parts: dispersed fat, a continuous water phase and an emulsifier
explains why droplet size and steady agitation decide how stable the sauce is
gives the window where butter and yolk sauces break, above roughly 85 C for a hollandaise
apply: mounts a pan sauce with cold butter off the heat, a cube at a time, and keeps it glossy
builds a vinaigrette at 3 parts oil to 1 part acid with mustard and holds it through service
rescues a broken sauce by restarting with a spoonful of intact base and whisking the split sauce back in
discriminate: separates a sauce held by emulsion from one thickened by reduction or by starch
separates a broken sauce from a merely thin one and gives the fix for each
separates a temporary emulsion from one stabilised by an emulsifier

title: Stocks
summary: Water drawn through bones, mirepoix and aromatics below a simmer, so gelatin and flavour come out without emulsifying the fat into the liquid.

misconceptions.text: A hard boil pulls more flavour out of the bones.

explain: explains why a stock is never boiled: it emulsifies the fat and clouds the pot
gives working times, roughly four hours for veal or beef and forty five minutes for fish
states the standard mirepoix, two parts onion to one carrot and one celery by weight
apply: holds the pot at 82 to 90 C and skims the scum through the first thirty minutes
strains through a chinois without pressing, then chills it fast in a shallow tray
judges the finished stock by the set on a chilled spoonful, not by tasting it hot
discriminate: separates a white stock from a brown stock by how the bones were treated
separates stock from broth by what goes in the pot and how the result is used
separates cloudiness caused by boiling from cloudiness caused by unskimmed scum

title: Roux
summary: Equal weights of flour and fat cooked together so the starch hydrates cleanly, taken from white through blond to brown as thickening power falls away.

misconceptions.text: A darker roux thickens more than a pale one.

explain: states the 1:1 ratio by weight and explains why it is weighed rather than scooped
explains what cooking out the flour removes and how long it takes
explains why a brown roux thickens less than a white one
apply: cooks a blond roux for about five minutes, then adds liquid in stages to a smooth base
uses roughly 100 g of roux per litre for a medium sauce and adjusts on the spoon
avoids lumps by matching temperatures and whisking steadily as the liquid goes in
discriminate: separates roux from a slurry or a beurre manie by when it is added and how it cooks out
separates a pasty sauce from an under thickened one
separates white, blond and brown roux by cooking time and by use

title: Thickeners
summary: The working set beyond roux: cornstarch slurry, beurre manie, gelatin, purees and reduction, each with its own gloss, clarity and tolerance for heat.

misconceptions.text: Cornstarch and flour thicken the same way at the same weight.

explain: states that cornstarch thickens at roughly twice the power of flour by weight
explains why cornstarch gives a clear gloss where flour gives an opaque sauce
explains why a starch sauce that has thinned cannot be fixed by boiling it longer
apply: stirs a cold slurry into a simmering sauce and cooks it out for a minute
finishes a sauce at the pass with beurre manie when it is a touch thin
chooses the thickener by what service needs: clarity, hold time and reheating
discriminate: separates a starch thickened sauce from an emulsion by how each one fails
separates roux from a slurry by when each is introduced
separates a sauce thinned by enzyme activity from one that was never thickened enough

title: Deglazing
summary: Dissolving the browned fond off the bottom of the pan with wine, stock or vinegar, so the crust that formed under the protein becomes the base of the sauce.

misconceptions.text: Black bits in the pan are just extra flavour.

explain: explains what fond is and why it sticks to the pan
explains why the liquid goes in while the pan is hot and how that lifts the fond
explains why burnt fond makes the sauce bitter and cannot be rescued
apply: pours off excess fat, then deglazes off the flame and scrapes with a wooden spoon
cooks the alcohol out of the wine before the stock goes in
reads the pan first and starts again when the fond is black rather than brown
discriminate: separates deglazing from simply adding liquid to a pan
separates brown fond worth lifting from burnt fond that has to be discarded
separates the deglaze from the reduction that follows it

title: Pan sauces
summary: A sauce built in the pan the protein just left: fond, deglaze, reduce, mount with cold butter, season and send, inside a few minutes.

misconceptions.text: A pan sauce needs cream to stop it splitting.

explain: names the sequence: fond, deglaze, reduce, mount, season
explains why the butter goes in cold and off the heat
explains why a pan sauce is made to order rather than held on the stove
apply: reduces the deglazed liquid by about half before anything is mounted into it
mounts roughly 30 to 60 g of cold butter per portion, swirling rather than whisking hard
corrects with salt and acid and tastes again before the sauce leaves the pan
discriminate: separates a pan sauce from a mother sauce by where the body comes from
separates a sauce that has split from one that is simply too thin
separates a sauce that needs more reduction from one that needs more butter

title: Mother sauces
summary: The classical bases, bechamel, veloute, espagnole, tomate and hollandaise, and the small sauces built on top of each one.

misconceptions.text: Every sauce in a restaurant is a derivative of a mother sauce.

explain: names the five bases and the thickener behind each one
explains what a small sauce adds to the mother it comes from
explains why hollandaise sits apart from the roux based sauces
apply: builds a veloute from a blond roux and a light stock and cooks it out for twenty minutes
derives a small sauce, a supreme for example, by finishing a veloute with cream
holds a bechamel under a cartouche or a film of butter so it does not skin
discriminate: separates a mother sauce from a pan sauce by how the body is built
separates a veloute from a bechamel by the liquid each one starts with
separates a derivative sauce from a new sauce

title: Acid balance
summary: Vinegar, citrus, wine and fermented ingredients used to cut fat and lift a dish, in small increments, where more salt would not help.

misconceptions.text: Adding acid just makes the dish taste sour.

explain: explains what acid does to perceived richness and sweetness
names three acids and what each brings besides sourness
explains why acid goes in at the end and in small increments
apply: lifts a flat, fatty sauce with a few drops of vinegar and tastes again before adding more
balances a dressing by tasting it on the ingredient it will dress, not off the spoon
pulls back a reduction that has gone sharp with fat, sweetness or more stock
discriminate: separates a dish that needs salt from one that needs acid
separates brightness from sourness in a finished sauce
separates acid used for balance from acid used to cure or to denature

title: Tasting and adjusting
summary: The loop that closes every dish: taste, name what is missing, change one thing, taste again, and write down what the fix was.

misconceptions.text: Tasting once before the plate goes out is enough.

explain: names the axes and the order they are checked in: salt, acid, fat, sweetness, texture, temperature
explains why only one change at a time teaches you anything
explains palate fatigue and how to reset between tastes
apply: tastes from a clean spoon, names the missing axis, makes one change and tastes again
tastes the dish as it will be eaten, with its garnish and at serving temperature
records the correction so the next service starts closer to right
discriminate: separates a dish that is flat from one that is under salted
separates a fault in a component from a fault in the assembly
separates a matter of preference from an actual fault when two cooks disagree

title: Plating
summary: Composing the plate for the guest and for the pass: hot food on hot plates, clean rims, and a layout that survives the walk to the table.

misconceptions.text: Plating is decoration you add at the end if there is time.

explain: explains why plate temperature matters as much as the arrangement
explains how the placement of the sauce changes the first bite
explains why everything on the plate has to be edible and deliberate
apply: plates the same dish twice to the same footprint and the same weight
wipes the rim and checks the plate under the pass light before it goes
plates in an order that keeps nothing waiting: sauce, protein, garnish
discriminate: separates a plate that reads clean from one that is merely empty
separates a garnish that adds flavour from one that only adds height
separates a plating problem from a cooking problem when a dish comes back

title: Menu planning
summary: Designing a menu the kitchen can actually execute: shared prep, station load at peak, contribution margin and what is in season.

misconceptions.text: A longer menu sells more covers.

explain: explains cross utilisation of prep across dishes
explains why the menu is limited by station load at peak rather than by the recipe list
explains contribution margin per dish against food cost percentage
apply: maps every dish to its station and finds the bottleneck at peak covers
prices a dish from a costed recipe with a target margin and a waste allowance
cuts or reworks a dish that shares no prep with anything else on the menu
discriminate: separates a menu problem from an execution problem when tickets back up
separates food cost percentage from contribution margin per plate
separates seasonality from novelty as a reason to change a dish

title: Cost control
summary: Yield, trim, portioning and costed recipes: knowing what a plate costs before it is sold, and where the money leaves the building.

misconceptions.text: Food cost is fixed by buying cheaper ingredients.

explain: defines yield percentage and shows where trim loss lands in a costed recipe
explains portion control as the link between the recipe and the plate cost
explains why waste, staff food and comps belong in the number
apply: costs a dish from purchase price through yield to plated cost
portions by weight at the station rather than by eye
tracks waste for a week and names the two largest sources
discriminate: separates a yield problem from a purchasing problem
separates food cost percentage from gross margin per plate
separates waste that is trim from waste that is spoilage

title: Food safety
summary: Keeping food out of the 5 to 63 C danger zone, cooking to a verified core temperature, and keeping raw product away from anything ready to eat.

misconceptions.text: Rinsing raw chicken washes the bacteria off.

explain: states the danger zone, 5 to 63 C, and what the time limits inside it are
gives a verified cook temperature such as 75 C for poultry, or 70 C held for two minutes
explains why rinsing raw poultry spreads bacteria around the sink instead of removing it
apply: probes the thickest part of the product and records the reading in the log
cools cooked food from 60 to 21 C within two hours and to 5 C within four more
labels and dates everything that leaves its original packaging
discriminate: separates a time and temperature failure from a cross contamination failure
separates food that is safe to serve from food that merely looks and smells fine
separates cleaning from sanitising and says what each step removes

title: Cross contamination
summary: Pathogens moving from raw product to ready to eat food along hands, boards, cloths, probes and shared utensils.

misconceptions.text: Wiping the board with a cloth between tasks is enough.

explain: names the usual routes: hands, boards, cloths, probes and shared utensils
explains why colour coded boards only work if the whole station keeps to them
explains the difference between cleaning a surface and sanitising it
apply: stores raw protein below ready to eat food in the fridge, never above it
changes gloves and washes hands between raw and cooked handling
sanitises the probe between products instead of wiping it on a cloth
discriminate: separates a cross contamination incident from an allergen transfer
separates a cleaned surface from a sanitised one
separates a batch that has to be discarded from one that can still be cooked through

title: Allergen handling
summary: Treating a declared allergen as a separate workflow: a dedicated station, clean tools, a checked ingredient deck and a spoken handover on every ticket.

misconceptions.text: You can pick the nuts off the plate and send it.

explain: explains why an allergen is dose sensitive in a way a pathogen count is not
explains why removing the visible allergen does not make the plate safe
says where the ingredient deck lives and who is responsible for keeping it current
apply: plates an allergen ticket at a dedicated station with clean tools and a fresh pan
reads the ingredient deck for the sauce instead of trusting memory
calls the allergen ticket out loud and hears it confirmed back at the pass
discriminate: separates an allergen incident from a general hygiene failure
separates a trace risk from a declared ingredient on the plate
separates a dish that can be adapted from one that has to be refused

title: Cold chain
summary: Unbroken refrigeration from the delivery door to the plate, chilled at or below 5 C and frozen at minus 18 C, logged rather than assumed.

misconceptions.text: Food that still feels cold can go back in the freezer.

explain: gives the working targets: 5 C or below chilled, minus 18 C frozen
explains why a delivery is probed at the door rather than after it is put away
explains why thawing on the bench is a break in the cold chain
apply: probes a delivery and rejects chilled goods that arrive above 8 C
thaws under refrigeration on a tray, below anything ready to eat
logs the walk in temperature at set times and escalates a drift within the shift
discriminate: separates a cold chain break from a cooking temperature failure
separates the air temperature in the walk in from the core temperature of the product
separates stock that has to be discarded from stock that can be cooked immediately

title: Temperature control
summary: Measuring and holding the temperature of the food itself: calibrated probes, hot holding above 63 C and cooking to a verified core.

misconceptions.text: The probe reads the true temperature the moment it touches the food.

explain: explains probe calibration in iced water at 0 C and in boiling water at 100 C
states hot holding above 63 C and explains why that is a holding number, not a target
explains why the core reading is taken at the thickest point, away from bone
apply: calibrates the probe at the start of the shift and records the check
holds sauces above 63 C or works in small batches remade every hour
re-probes after resting so carryover is part of the reading
discriminate: separates the temperature of the food from the temperature of the equipment
separates hot holding from cooking and from reheating
separates a probe that has drifted from a product that is genuinely cold

title: Service timing
summary: Sequencing tickets so every component of every plate on a table lands at the pass hot and at the same moment.

misconceptions.text: Start every dish on the ticket at the same time.

explain: explains firing backwards from the component with the longest cook time
explains what a fire, a pickup and a hold each mean at the pass
explains why a table is timed as a whole rather than plate by plate
apply: fires a table of four with different cook times so the plates land together
calls a hold on the station that has run ahead of the others
rebuilds the order of the board when a table adds a course mid service
discriminate: separates a timing failure from a capacity failure
separates a dish that is late from one that was fired late
separates holding a plate from remaking it

title: Kitchen communication
summary: The spoken protocol of a working line: calls and callbacks, corners and hot pans, and saying the problem out loud while it is still small.

misconceptions.text: A quiet line is a line in control.

explain: explains why every call gets a callback
names the standard calls, behind, corner, hot, sharp, and what each one prevents
explains why a problem called early costs less than one found at the pass
apply: repeats the ticket back to the expediter word for word
calls a shortfall the moment it is known rather than at pickup
hands the station over with a spoken list of what is down and what is prepped
discriminate: separates a communication failure from a timing failure
separates a call that carries information from one that only adds noise
separates escalating to the chef from quietly working around the problem

title: Fermentation
summary: Controlled microbial transformation steered by salt, temperature and time, from a 2 percent vegetable brine to a levain.

misconceptions.text: Fermented food is just controlled spoilage and is never really safe.

explain: explains why a 2 percent brine selects for lactic acid bacteria
explains how temperature changes both the speed and the flavour of a ferment
explains what a pH below 4.6 means for safety
apply: brines vegetables at 2 percent by weight and keeps everything under the surface
tracks a ferment by taste, smell and pH rather than by the number of days
moves the jar to the fridge to hold the flavour once it is where it should be
discriminate: separates a healthy ferment from spoilage by smell, colour and pH
separates kahm yeast from mould
separates a lactic ferment from an alcoholic one

title: Bread basics
summary: Flour, water, salt and leavening read as baker's percentages, developed by time or by mixing, and baked with steam for the first minutes.

misconceptions.text: Bread dough always needs long kneading.

explain: reads a formula in baker's percentages with the flour at 100 percent
explains hydration and what a 65 percent dough feels like next to an 80 percent one
explains what steam in the first minutes does to oven spring and to the crust
apply: mixes a 70 percent hydration dough and develops it with folds instead of long kneading
proofs to the dough rather than to the clock and checks it with the poke test
bakes with steam for the first fifteen minutes, then dry to set the crust
discriminate: separates under proofed dough from over proofed dough by crumb and by spring
separates a hydration problem from a development problem
separates commercial yeast from a levain in timing and in flavour

title: Pastry basics
summary: The pastry disciplines that reward weighing and cold hands: 3:2:1 shortcrust, laminated dough, and custards that set at a temperature.

misconceptions.text: You can adjust pastry by feel the way you adjust a sauce.

explain: states the 3:2:1 shortcrust ratio by weight, flour to fat to water
explains why cold fat gives a flaky texture where warm fat gives a sandy one
explains why a creme anglaise sets in a narrow window around 82 to 84 C
apply: makes a shortcrust with cold butter and rests it before rolling and again before baking
cooks a creme anglaise to 82 to 84 C and strains it straight into a cold bowl
blind bakes with weight until the base is set and coloured before the filling goes in
discriminate: separates a tough crust from a sandy one and names the cause of each
separates a custard that curdled from one that never set
separates a chemical leavener from a mechanical one

title: Block ciphers
summary: A keyed, reversible permutation on one fixed size block, such as AES on 128 bits, which says nothing about longer messages and authenticates nothing.

misconceptions.text: If a ciphertext decrypts without error, it must have been encrypted with my key.

explain: states that the cipher maps one fixed size block to another under a key and back again
says that the map is bijective, so every block is a valid ciphertext for some plaintext
separates the primitive from a mode of operation, which is what handles longer messages
apply: encrypts and decrypts a single block with a chosen key and predicts the output length
picks a mode of operation rather than calling the raw primitive on a long message
refuses to treat a successful decryption as proof of origin
discriminate: separates the block cipher from the mode that uses it
separates confidentiality from integrity and names which one the primitive gives
gives one case where a tampered ciphertext still decrypts to something

title: Counter mode
summary: Turning a block cipher into a stream cipher by encrypting a counter block per position and XORing the result with the plaintext, so the keystream, not the cipher, does the encrypting.

misconceptions.text: In counter mode the plaintext blocks are the input to the block cipher.

explain: describes the counter block, its increment, and the keystream it produces
states that encryption is the XOR of plaintext and keystream, and that XOR is its own inverse
explains why the counter block must differ per message, which is what the nonce is for
apply: derives the plaintext of a second message from a known plaintext and ciphertext pair under a repeated keystream
computes a keystream block from the counter and the key
chooses a fresh nonce per message under one key
discriminate: separates the keystream from the ciphertext and from the block cipher output
separates a repeated key, which is fine, from a repeated keystream, which is not
gives one case where counter mode keeps a message secret and still lets it be altered

title: Galois field arithmetic
summary: Addition and multiplication in a finite field such as GF(2^128), where addition is XOR and multiplication is polynomial multiplication reduced by a fixed irreducible polynomial.

misconceptions.text: Multiplying two field elements is the same as multiplying the two 128-bit integers.

explain: states that the field has a finite number of elements and that addition is the XOR of the two elements
describes multiplication as polynomial multiplication followed by reduction modulo a fixed polynomial
says why a 128-bit block can be read as an element of GF(2^128)
apply: adds two 128-bit elements by XOR and predicts the result
multiplies two small elements and reduces the product by the field polynomial
reads a polynomial equation over the field as an ordinary equation in one unknown
discriminate: separates field addition from integer addition with carries
separates the reduction polynomial from the elements being multiplied
gives one case where the field result differs from the integer result

title: Message authentication
summary: A short tag computed with a secret key over a message, so a recipient can tell that the message came from a key holder and was not altered on the way.

misconceptions.text: If a message is encrypted, nobody can change it without me noticing.

explain: states what a tag proves: origin among the key holders, and that the bytes are unaltered
says that the tag is keyed, so an attacker without the key cannot recompute it
explains why a hash with no key is not a message authentication tag
apply: verifies a tag before using the message it covers
authenticates the associated data as well as the ciphertext when the format carries both
rejects a message whose tag does not check, rather than reading it first
discriminate: separates authentication, which detects change, from encryption, which hides content
separates an unkeyed hash from a keyed tag
gives one case where a ciphertext is secret and still forgeable

title: Authenticated encryption
summary: One construction that both hides a message and authenticates it, usually with associated data left in the clear, so a recipient gets secrecy and integrity from a single key.

misconceptions.text: Authenticated encryption is encryption with a hash of the plaintext appended.

explain: names the two guarantees, secrecy and integrity, and says which part of the construction gives each
explains what associated data is and why it is authenticated but not encrypted
states that the tag is checked before the plaintext is used
apply: encrypts with a fresh nonce and transmits nonce, ciphertext and tag together
puts routing or header data in the associated data instead of leaving it unauthenticated
treats a failed tag check as a hard error
discriminate: separates authenticated encryption from a bare mode of operation with no tag
separates the tag from the ciphertext and says what each one protects
gives one case where a scheme keeps a message secret and still accepts a forgery

title: Nonce misuse
summary: What a repeated nonce costs. Under one key a reused nonce repeats the keystream and, in a polynomial tag scheme, exposes the hash key, so both secrecy and forgery resistance are lost.

misconceptions.text: A nonce is safe as long as an attacker cannot guess it.

explain: states that a nonce must be unique under a key, and that secrecy and randomness are not what makes it safe
explains why a repeated keystream lets one known plaintext reveal another message
explains why the per nonce value cancels between two tags and leaves an equation in the hash key
apply: recovers a second plaintext from a known pair encrypted under the same key and nonce
builds the polynomial from two tags and their blocks and solves it for the hash key
chooses a nonce strategy, counter or random with a size argument, that cannot repeat under one key
discriminate: separates a repeated nonce from a repeated key
separates the loss of secrecy from the loss of forgery resistance and says how each one happens
gives one case where a nonce is unpredictable and still unsafe because it repeats

title: CPU and RAM
summary: The division of labour a computer is built on: RAM holds the machine code and the data, and the CPU fetches instructions from it and executes them, keeping a little state in registers.

misconceptions.text: The processor reads a program off the disk and runs it from there.

explain: says that machine code has to be in RAM before the CPU can run it
names registers as the small, very fast storage the CPU keeps its own state in
separates an opcode and its operands from the assembly text a human reads
apply: points at where a running program and the kernel both live at once
reads a short assembly listing and says which bytes are the opcode
names the register that holds the address of the next instruction
discriminate: separates RAM from a disk and says which one the CPU can fetch from
separates a register from a memory address
separates machine code from the assembly written to stand for it

title: Fetch-execute cycle
summary: The loop the processor never leaves: read the instruction the pointer names, execute it, move the pointer, repeat, with no notion of programs or of an operating system.

misconceptions.text: The processor knows which processes are running and switches between them itself.

explain: describes fetch, execute and the move of the instruction pointer as one repeating loop
says that a jump is nothing but a write to the instruction pointer
states that a process is an operating system abstraction the CPU never sees
apply: traces a short sequence of instructions and says where the pointer is after each
explains a conditional branch as a choice of what to put in the pointer
says what has to happen for the processor to start running a program that was just loaded
discriminate: separates what the CPU tracks from what the kernel tracks
separates sequential execution from the illusion of several programs at once
separates a jump instruction from a call into the operating system

title: Privilege rings
summary: The mode a processor runs in, kernel or user, which decides what instructions and what memory the running code is allowed to touch, held in a register the code cannot raise on its own.

misconceptions.text: A program that needs more access can switch itself into kernel mode.

explain: names kernel mode and user mode and what each one may do
says that the mode is held in a processor register, on x86-64 the low bits of cs
states that the processor starts in kernel mode and the kernel drops to user mode to run a program
apply: reads a privilege level out of a given cs value
says which ring the kernel, a driver and an application run in
names one instruction a user mode program is not allowed to execute
discriminate: separates the mode the processor is in from the request a program makes to cross it
separates the four architectural rings from the two that are actually used
separates a privilege level from a memory permission

title: Interrupts
summary: A numbered entry into code the kernel registered in advance: the processor looks the number up in a vector table, switches mode and jumps there, and returns to where it was when the handler is done.

misconceptions.text: The code that raises an interrupt chooses the address the processor jumps to.

explain: describes the interrupt vector table as a map from interrupt numbers to handler pointers
says the table is registered with the CPU at boot and can only be written from kernel mode
names the pair of instructions that enter a handler and return from it
apply: follows one interrupt from the instruction that raises it to the handler and back
says what the processor does with the instruction pointer on the way in and on the way out
names where the caller has to put data the handler will need
discriminate: separates a software interrupt raised by an instruction from a hardware one raised by a device
separates the interrupt mechanism from the system call built on top of it
separates an interrupt from an ordinary jump or call

title: System calls
summary: The standard way a user mode program asks the kernel to act for it: arguments go in registers, an instruction hands control to code the kernel chose, and the kernel returns to user mode with an answer.

misconceptions.text: A system call is an ordinary function call into kernel code: the program jumps into the kernel the way it jumps into a library function.

explain: says that a system call is a controlled transition from user space into kernel code, not a jump the program chooses
names the mechanism underneath, a software interrupt or a dedicated instruction, and how arguments are passed
explains that libc and ntdll wrap that mechanism, and that calling the wrapper is still an ordinary function call
apply: traces one call such as open or exit from the library function down to the mode switch and back
names where the call number and the arguments are placed before control is handed over
says why the same C program works on two machines whose syscall mechanisms differ
discriminate: separates a library call, which stays in user mode, from the system call inside it
separates the request a program makes from the privilege level it runs at
separates the syscall interface from the interrupt mechanism that carries it

title: Instruction sets
summary: What a processor architecture offers as instructions, and the CISC and RISC habits behind that choice: many specialised instructions on one side, a small uniform set on the other.

misconceptions.text: A dedicated system call instruction does something different from an interrupt, not the same thing faster.

explain: says what an instruction set is and that machine code is written against one architecture
contrasts the CISC habit of adding specialised instructions with the RISC habit of keeping few
gives the system call instructions as an example of a common operation given its own opcode
apply: names which instruction a 64-bit program on x86-64 would use for a system call and why
says what an AArch64 program uses instead
explains why a binary built for one architecture does not run on another
discriminate: separates the instruction set from the microarchitecture that implements it
separates a faster path to the kernel from a different privilege outcome
separates assembly, which is text, from the encoding an architecture defines
